_officialAuthorityConfirmation: The review's readiness record carries official_authority_refresh_required, and Oklahoma is the one state in this wave where the refresh did not close the top research item. The review's overall jurisdiction decision is "Additional research required before implementation", and its stated reason is Senate Bill 2030, passed in May 2026, which amends both operative statutes. Retrieval was attempted at the Oklahoma Legislature on 2026-08-06: the bill information record for SB 2030 in the 2026 session was located, but the enrolled text was not obtained from that channel, so 22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19 as amended have not been read. That matters more in Oklahoma than the same gap would elsewhere, because section 18 was last amended by Chapter 259, O.S.L. 2024 and section 19 by Chapter 292, O.S.L. 2025 before SB 2030 amended both again, so the category structure has moved in three consecutive years and any logic built on a pre-2024 reading is stale in three separate directions. The review's own instruction, to screen by category description rather than by paragraph number, is adopted throughout for exactly that reason and is the single best judgment call in the document. What the refresh did close, it closed at the responsible agency's own channel. The Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation's Criminal History Record Expungement page was read on 2026-08-06 and confirms two of the review's headline findings word for word. On fees: "Expunging your court record is free." "Expunging your arrest record requires paying a $150 processing fee. It may also require fees be paid to local law enforcement agencies expunging their records." "The OSBI accepts cashier's checks or money orders. Personal checks WILL NOT be accepted." On the section 991c distinction, which the review calls the most important consumer-facing point in Oklahoma: "A Section 991(c) expungement will not expunge (remove) the arrest record." That confirmation is carried structurally rather than as a warning, by making the arrest-record screen a required component of the section 991c node. The same page corroborates the Clean Slate status the review records: it refers to Clean Slate eligibility by category and links to a Clean Slate page, and does not state that automatic sealing is operating or that an expedited request portal exists, which is consistent with the November 1, 2027 date the review records from SB 2030 for OSBI to begin sealing and with the portal being required but not yet built. Both SB 2030 nodes are therefore normalized as guidance and monitoring rather than as routes a participant can use today. The consequence for the petition tracks is deliberate and is the shape of this memo: they are implementable, because the petition framework is well understood, the review documents it capably and SB 2030 expressly preserves the right to petition, but each one leads with a free-route screen that stops rather than concludes. The review's warning is the reason: building against the pre-SB 2030 text risks generating paid petitions for people who could have used a free route, and risks telling people they are Clean Slate eligible when the amendment removed them. Sections 18 and 19 as amended have now been read. The enrolled text of Senate Bill 2030 was obtained from the Oklahoma Legislature on 2026-08-07 and the codified 22 O.S. § 18 was read at the Oklahoma State Courts Network the same day, which supplied the chapter number, the effective date and independent confirmation that the clean-slate subsection was repealed. The Act is Laws 2026, c. 282, effective 1 July 2026. It amends §§ 18 and 19, creates §§ 18b and 19d, repeals a duplicate § 18, and leaves §§ 19a, 60.18 and 991c untouched. Eligibility for sealing without a petition exists from the effective date under § 18b(B), subject to the availability of funds; administration does not, the Bureau being required to establish the request portal by 1 November 2026, to begin the automatic process on or before 1 November 2027 and to complete then-eligible electronic records before 1 November 2029. The eligible set was widened rather than narrowed, and the right to petition is expressly preserved by § 19d(G). No participant is told they are Clean Slate eligible, because eligibility is funding-conditioned and no process is operating. Scope note: this correction owns ok_clean_slate and ok_osbi_portal only. The eight petition tracks still carry the pre-correction statement that the enrolled text was not obtained, and still cite the ten-year obliteration rule as § 19(N) where the amended section carries it at § 19(L); those are left value-identical here and are recorded for a separate owner.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge a Non-Conviction or Innocence Record (22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Oklahoma arrest that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: The section 18 categories include records where the person was not charged, was acquitted, was factually innocent, or where the charge was dismissed. The petition goes to the district court in the county where the arrest information is located, the court gives thirty days' notice to the prosecuting agency, the arresting agency, the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation and any other agency holding relevant records, and the standard is a balancing test: the court may seal if the harm to privacy or the danger of unwarranted adverse consequences outweighs the public interest in retaining the records. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge a Misdemeanor Conviction (22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19)

controllingAuthority.summary: The section 18 categories provide petition routes for misdemeanour convictions on stated waiting periods and prior-record conditions. Because section 18 has been amended in three consecutive years and renumbered, the screen runs on the category description rather than the paragraph number, which is the review's single best judgment call and is preserved here. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate Sealing Without Petition (22 O.S. §§ 18b and 19d, as enacted by Senate Bill 2030, Laws 2026, c. 282)
tracks.publicName: Oklahoma's automatic record sealing, and where it stands

controllingAuthority.summary: Senate Bill 2030 was enacted and is in force. It was approved by the Governor on 11 May 2026 after the emergency was adopted in both chambers, it is codified as Laws 2026, c. 282, and the codifier records the amendment as effective 1 July 2026. The Act amends 22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19, creates 22 O.S. §§ 18b and 19d, and repeals a duplicate § 18. Sections 19a, 60.18 and 991c are untouched. The former § 18(C) route — automatic sealing of clean slate eligible ARREST records, on a trigger that had already passed — was repealed, and the § 19(B) machinery that ran it was removed. Eligibility now sits in § 18b and the process in § 19d. Section 18b(B) provides that "Beginning on the effective date of this act and subject to the availability of funds, individuals with clean slate eligible records shall be eligible to have their records sealed without filing a court petition." So statutory eligibility exists today; administration does not. Section 19d(A) requires the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation to establish a publicly accessible online portal for expedited expungement requests by 1 November 2026. Section 19d(D) requires the Bureau to begin implementing the automatic process on or before 1 November 2027, and requires all electronic records eligible through that process on or after 1 November 2027 to be identified and expunged before 1 November 2029. The Act widened the eligible set rather than narrowing it. Section 18b reaches records rather than arrest records only, expressly including court records, sets a temporal floor of 1 January 1980, carries forward the new § 18(A)(15) identity-theft category, and adds two conviction categories the repealed route never reached at all: a 63 O.S. § 2-402(A)(1) felony where the person is not currently serving a sentence, five years have passed since the end of the last felony or misdemeanour sentence and the record is single-source; and a misdemeanour conviction with no felony conviction, no pending charges, five years since the end of the last misdemeanour sentence and a single-source record. What it removed was the earlier, narrower route, not a participant's category. Neither the automatic process nor the portal is operating. The Bureau's own criminal history record expungement page, last updated 23 July 2026 and therefore after the Act took effect, describes no portal and does not state that automatic sealing is operating. Both statutory deadlines are in the future. The right to petition is expressly preserved. Section 19d(G) reads "Nothing in this section precludes an individual from filing a petition with the district court pursuant to Section 19 of Title 22 of the Oklahoma Statutes for expungement of clean slate eligible records", and § 19(A) is undisturbed. The petition routes are the only routes an Oklahoma participant can use today. Records sealed through the clean slate route are PARTIALLY sealed under § 18b(D): unavailable to the public, still available to law enforcement for law enforcement purposes, and still admissible under § 18b(E) to prove a prior conviction or deferred judgment without an unsealing order. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing. Title 22 § 19 does not authorise physical destruction, a sealed record may be unsealed on changed conditions or a compelling reason, and under § 19(L) — the ten-year obliteration rule, which the pre-2026 lettering carried further down the section — a sealed record not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed.

exclusions: Everyone, as a route to use today. Statutory eligibility exists under 22 O.S. § 18b(B), but the automatic process is not operating and the request portal is not published.

The participant is told the true position: statutory eligibility exists, administration does not yet, and the petition route remains open and expressly preserved by § 19d(G) in the meantime.

Eligibility for sealing without a petition exists now under § 18b(B) and is subject to the availability of funds; the process under § 19d does not begin until the Bureau implements it, which the statute requires on or before 1 November 2027, with completion for then-eligible electronic records before 1 November 2029. A participant who has heard that Oklahoma clears records automatically is told what is actually true and is screened for the petition routes rather than left waiting.

What the route is and is not, which is the half a participant is most likely to get wrong. Senate Bill 2030 widened the eligible set rather than narrowing it: § 18b reaches records including court records rather than arrest records only, and adds two conviction categories the repealed § 18(C) route never reached. But the sealing is PARTIAL under § 18b(D) — the record stays available to law enforcement and stays admissible under § 18b(E) to prove a prior conviction — several categories require an Oklahoma single-source record, and the route reaches nothing before 1 January 1980. The reason to look at the petition routes is the timetable and these limits, not a lost category.

What is tracked and when: the 1 November 2026 portal deadline under § 19d(A), the 1 November 2027 date on which the Bureau must have begun the automatic process under § 19d(D), the 1 November 2029 completion date, the annual report the Bureau must publish and submit to the Legislature from 2027, any appropriation reaching § 18b(B), any rules promulgated under § 19d(E)(7), and the Bureau's own Clean Slate and expungement pages. Re-checked before every release.

tracks.legalName: OSBI Expedited Expungement Request Portal (22 O.S. § 19d, as enacted by Senate Bill 2030, Laws 2026, c. 282)
tracks.publicName: Oklahoma's free expungement request portal, and where it stands

controllingAuthority.summary: Senate Bill 2030 was enacted and is in force. It was approved by the Governor on 11 May 2026 after the emergency was adopted in both chambers, it is codified as Laws 2026, c. 282, and the codifier records the amendment as effective 1 July 2026. The Act amends 22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19, creates 22 O.S. §§ 18b and 19d, and repeals a duplicate § 18. Sections 19a, 60.18 and 991c are untouched. Section 19d(A) requires the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation to establish and maintain a publicly accessible online portal by 1 November 2026 for individuals to submit an expedited expungement request for clean slate eligible records as defined in § 18b, or records eligible under § 18(A)(16). Section 19d(B) limits what the request may require to sufficient personal identification information for the Bureau to locate the record and contact information for notification. Section 19d(C) sets the review sequence: the Bureau reviews the record, solicits review by the arresting and prosecuting agencies, sends a request to the district court on confirmation, and where any party finds the record ineligible sends the individual a written or electronic notice of rejection stating the reasons. The statute sets no fee for the request. Neither the automatic process nor the portal is operating. The Bureau's own criminal history record expungement page, last updated 23 July 2026 and therefore after the Act took effect, describes no portal and does not state that automatic sealing is operating. Both statutory deadlines are in the future. The right to petition is expressly preserved. Section 19d(G) reads "Nothing in this section precludes an individual from filing a petition with the district court pursuant to Section 19 of Title 22 of the Oklahoma Statutes for expungement of clean slate eligible records", and § 19(A) is undisturbed. The petition routes are the only routes an Oklahoma participant can use today. Records sealed through the clean slate route are PARTIALLY sealed under § 18b(D): unavailable to the public, still available to law enforcement for law enforcement purposes, and still admissible under § 18b(E) to prove a prior conviction or deferred judgment without an unsealing order. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing. Title 22 § 19 does not authorise physical destruction, a sealed record may be unsealed on changed conditions or a compelling reason, and under § 19(L) — the ten-year obliteration rule, which the pre-2026 lettering carried further down the section — a sealed record not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed.

exclusions: Everyone, as a route to use today. No portal is published and nothing can be submitted through one.
Any record outside the § 18b(A) clean slate eligible set or § 18(A)(16), which are the only records the portal reaches.

destination.name: The Oklahoma district court
destination.detail: Title 22 § 4A defines 'court' as the Oklahoma district court unless a contrary intention appears, so 'court of conviction' is not a complete universal destination, particularly for a municipal record or a charge with no conviction. Recommended ordinary venue: the district court for the district or county holding the relevant arrest information, consistent with § 19(A); § 19c expressly incorporates § 19(B)–(M), not § 19(A), so that venue conclusion is an interpretation of the combined statutory structure, not a quotation from § 19c. A municipal-origin record, records spanning counties, or disputed docketing requires court or counsel confirmation of the district filing and case type for the precise record; that does not make the destination unknown. rules.filing: The defendant petitions the Oklahoma district court (or the court acts on its own motion) under 22 O.S. § 19c for good-cause expungement of a prostitution-related charge or conviction resulting from trafficking; the petition is filed in the district court for the county holding the relevant arrest information, with county and case-type docketing confirmed for the precise record. The remedy is limited: public sealing while preserving law-enforcement access, with the order identifying § 19c; it is not vacatur and not a promise that every trafficking-related offense is covered.
rules.fees: Kept separately sourced: OSBI distinguishes its arrest-record processing charge from court-record processing, which does not establish a universal $0 clerk filing fee; no route-specific fee waiver is adopted without enacted authority or an actual order.
rules.notice: Under 22 O.S. § 19 as amended by the enacted 2026 SB 2030 (notice provision renumbered to subsection B), the court sets the hearing and provides 30 days' notice to the prosecuting agency, the arresting agency, OSBI and other relevant persons or agencies; the participant asks the clerk how the court-directed notice is carried out and never certifies that notice occurred before it did.
rules.service: Court-directed notice under § 19(B); no participant service certified in advance.
rules.researchPacketComponents: Identified records and offenses; participant-provided trafficking and causal facts; good-cause grounds; the agency list; supporting evidence; a proposed § 19c order with public-sealing and law-enforcement-access limits; sensitive evidence through the applicable protected-filing mechanism, with no promise of a closed hearing or confidential petition merely because the subject is trafficking. These are proposed drafting components, not an official statewide form inventory.
rules.researchDoNotImplementHB3835: The official 2026 HB 3835 history records House passage and Senate committee referral, not enactment; its last published version is engrossed; its proposed provisions (broader coverage, no good cause, mandated fee waiver and closed hearings, changed proof and relief rules) are not operative law and its printed future effective date is not evidence of enactment. SB 2030, by contrast, records gubernatorial approval and its enrolled text supplies the operative § 19 amendment.

researchParticipantText.text: This route asks an Oklahoma district court to expunge specified prostitution-related records connected to human trafficking. It does not cover every offense simply because trafficking occurred, and relief is not automatic. The court must arrange the required agency notice and decides the request. An order under this route seals records from public access but does not make them unavailable to law enforcement.

It adds the point that makes this slot different from its equivalent in other states: tribal records are a live issue in Oklahoma post-McGirt and should be an explicit escalation.

destination.detail: The review states no filing actor and no destination. The matter is the outer boundary of Oklahoma relief, with tribal records singled out as a live post-McGirt issue requiring explicit escalation.

selfHelpStopConditions: Every request touching a federal, tribal, military or out-of-state record. Tribal records in particular are an explicit escalation in Oklahoma.

The review records tribal records as a live issue requiring escalation without surveying a route.

The slot is preserved as a deferred entry so that instruction has somewhere to live, and no output strategy is asserted because no route was surveyed. The escalation itself is carried as a stop condition and a self-help boundary on every implementable Oklahoma node.
